edges.effect_quant: The stronger recent cohorts show substantial infant protection. In Utah, maternal vaccination during pregnancy was associated with a relative risk of 0.30 for laboratory-confirmed influenza and 0.19 for infant influenza hospitalization under 6 months, while a large Ontario test-negative study estimated 64% effectiveness against laboratory-confirmed infant influenza.
edges.population: infants under 6 months born to pregnant women vaccinated against influenza during pregnancy
edges.mechanism: Maternal influenza vaccination raises maternal antibodies that cross the placenta and provide passive infant protection during the first months of life, when babies are too young to receive seasonal influenza vaccination themselves.
edges.summary: The evidence leans clearly protective for infant influenza prevention after maternal vaccination in pregnancy. Large North American observational studies and a smaller prospective infant cohort all report fewer lab-confirmed influenza infections in infants whose mothers were vaccinated while pregnant.
edges.caveats: Most of the evidence is observational or test-negative rather than randomized in current high-income settings, so residual confounding and season-specific vaccine match still matter. The benefit is strongest for the first 6 months of life and should not be interpreted as complete protection against all respiratory illness.
